Adler Airport, Sochi, Caucasus, Russia

Date: November 11, 1989

Time: daytime

A female witness named L. Suhareva arrived at Adler Airport located on the Black Sea coast to place her bags into the automatic baggage locker. There a strange “man” suddenly entered the room and confronted her. The man appeared to be about 25 years of age, taller than average, solidly built, disheveled hair and a pale, serious face. The stranger looked around the room in confusion, apparently searching for something. He wore a black leather jacket and jeans. His movements were slow and awkward sometimes appearing in slow motion. The “man” then examined the walls of the room, at one time peeping under a bench. He then noticed an electric socket (wall outlet) he poked into with his long wide-place fingers and ordered a man (Ivan) that was sitting nearby to move aside in clear Russian.

Everyone in the room was amazed at the behavior of the stranger and reproached him. He tried to say something but then waved his hand and walked out. Several minutes later he returned and leaning over looked into the wall socket again. He was then asked by another bystander name Edward, what was he looking for and mumbled something about a gift and scarf. Suhareva then asked the stranger if he had forgotten his locker number, or had not written it down, perhaps he was looking in the wrong area. In a bewildered look the stranger asked, “What is write down?" and mumbled some other incomprehensible words. Suhareva continued asking him questions and asked what town had he flown in from, the stranger answered “Sverdlovsk”

Asked if he came in by airplane or train, he thought for a minute, said "airplane" syllable by syllable and then as if reacting suddenly he yelled, “No, I descended by aggregate. You have different atmosphere here, strong pressure, I became ill”. The people in the room stared at him in amazement, some became frightened. But Suhareva preserved her self-control and asked the stranger, “What is aggregate? You mean by flying saucer don’t you?” The stranger then seemed to become angry, reiterating, “No! I descended by aggregate!” Then he leaned on Edward’s shoulder and asked for the wall socket, saying that he needed to “recharge”.

The stranger then sat on the bench in front of the outlet. Then he grabbed hold of the windowsill with his right hand and stuck his middle finger into the socket. He began to shake, his face now covered by strange blue spots. 10-15 seconds later he took his hand out of the socket and vigorously shook his head. The blue spots then vanished. The stranger then stood up and walked towards the door, saying, “That’s all, I remember now!” He was now speaking in a normal tone of voice. When the stranger walked out of the room, two of the men in the room, (Edward & Ivan) experienced severe headaches and asked who the stranger was. Suhareva was convinced that it had been an extraterrestrial.

EDIT: Source: Letter to several Russian & Ukrainian UFO Magazines and Newspapers, Anton Anfalov

A mass-realization of the interconnectedness of all things that allows humanity to transcend the limitations of the self and instead acknowledge that which hurts one hurts us all... To me, if universal love were universally accessible to all people, it would be a logical choice to choose it over not. In other words, only irrational actors would choose to behave outside that worldview.

But you're right that humans behaving rationally and logically is completely separate from the notion of universal love - especially in the context of personal choice. However, I believe that the free market of ideas might regulate the ones that choose to reject the option of universal love if it existed in the minds of the majority. To be clear, I am also not advocating that everyone must think alike - I can see the slippery slope here; I am just suggesting that at a basic level, if love and appreciation for all fellow human beings was a humanitarian norm that it would quickly gain a foothold due to the obvious benefits it has over the current system. Which is not to say that it would always remain that way - we human beings have short memories and until greed as a concept is such a foreign concept as to be unthinkable, it would have the potential to rise again and dominate - I tend to believe that it currently exists in all humans as a primitive instinct of self-preservation.

Once we all take care of each other though, that instinct will truly be fully antiquated. We won't get there in my lifetime or yours, but I do believe that you must be the change you want to see in the world and to find happiness in the little signs of success - it's the only thing you can truly appreciate.

People are wired to enjoy conflict though. People both like to dominate and to be dominated. Isn't that a bit of a hurdle? If universal love means shunning a good amount of things that human beings have historically have never shunned then couldn't that create a whole new type of perversion? When humans shun their sexuality it perverts them in some weird ways no? So what happens when a human shuns their violent nature and greed? Does this hurt our survivability in harsh situations? There is a time and place for every behavior humans have ever exhibited in the history of our shared awareness.

You buy one big good thing by adopting any viewpoint, but it's probably safe to say the loss in another arguably, just as important aspect of human behavior, might not make it worth it. It is the animals in us all that holds us back, but it is also the animal in us all that got us here to begin with. How do you weigh the value of the perceived negative aspects of human consciousnesses and behavior against the value of new behavior that we know could solve all our problems in a certain time and place?

I don't believe that. Adrenaline exists as a biological necessity to deal with a dangerous world. If that world becomes less dangerous, then we have less need for that adrenaline and should be happy about that. Unfortunately, due to social conditioning and old habits dying hard, rather than taking comfort in the fact that we live in a progressively safer world generation after generation, we convince ourselves that conflict is all around us and as you put it, convince ourselves that we "like conflict".

Humans have a tendency to dominate and be dominated, that much is true - but I wouldn't say that they like it. I believe everyone who dominates does so mostly for the same motivation - the (founded or unfounded) belief that they will be dominated if they don't dominate someone else. The hurdle is to convince everyone that we're all OK.

Regarding perversion, perhaps you are right, I'm not sure. I would say though, that it is about time that we, as humans try another approach, consequences be damned, if it means that we move away from violence and domination. Progress never comes without its own set of challenges. Survivability would definitely take a hit, but I believe that is a risk worth taking considering that our gravest threat is ourselves. In other words, I don't think the dolphins are going to rise up and overthrow us if we become less violent in general.

I'm not advocating any absolute viewpoint. All viewpoints should be constantly challenged. There is a time to plant and a time to uproot that which is planted. The animal got us to this point - and I am not without gratitude. We have overcome some huge obstacles and done some amazing things, providing a framework in which the humanity in us can come out and replace the animal as the driving force in the human being.
